commentary.bottom_line: Two studies report findings favoring sequenced AI adoption, but neither compares staged rollout with enterprise-wide deployment, so the effect of staging itself remains unmeasured. Support for the recommendation comes mainly from 38 endorsements, most of them frameworks and commentaries.

perspectives.view: One before-after study across 26 U.S. hospitals and one German simulation both favor sequenced adoption. The hospital study has no comparison group and cannot separate the effect of staging from the effect of the decision support tools. The simulation uses stylized parameters. Certainty is very low because of risk of bias and indirectness.

In the 26-hospital rollout, postoperative acute kidney injury fell from an average of 1,031 cases per month at baseline to 400 per month after Phase 3. Intraoperative hypotension episodes fell 33% in Phase 1. These results suggest early phases may show benefit before scaling, though background trends could explain part of the decline.

The simulation found that interoperability-led sequencing reduced midtransition volatility compared with automation-first sequencing. An uncoordinated transition produced the largest variation in turnaround and throughput. This suggests the order of rollout steps and site data readiness may matter alongside pacing. No study measured site readiness criteria directly.

Staged rollout delays system-wide returns and requires staff to run pilots, collect metrics, and decide when to advance. Executives cited in one endorsing guidance asked for standardized metrics to compare sites, which suggests demonstrated value lacks shared definitions today. The 26-hospital study shows a phased model can run at multi-site scale.

Neither study reports results by payer, language, or literacy. Two endorsing commentaries, on inclusive chatbots and machine-assisted translation, call for pilots and language-specific deployment before scaling. No test examined whether staging protects underserved sites or delays their access to useful tools.

commentary.research_gap: No study compares staged rollout with simultaneous enterprise-wide deployment on patient outcomes, cost, or clinician adoption, and none tests specific site readiness criteria or value thresholds for advancing between phases. A stepped-wedge or cluster-randomized design across sites could address both questions.
commentary.underserved_note: Neither study reported including Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations, and one was a simulation with no patients. Health systems cannot assume that readiness and value criteria developed at well-resourced sites will transfer to safety-net sites, which may also be scheduled last in a staged rollout.
